group.passage: One of the greatest abilities humans have is language. We have the ability to transmit our ideas across space and time. Since there isn’t just one language in the world — in fact, around 7,000 languages are spoken around the world, all of which differ in all kinds of ways, that begs the question: Does the language shape the way we think? While language relativity has been a century-old question, linguists have yet been unable to provide concrete scientific data. Recently, Lera Boroditsky, a cognitive scientist in UCSD, has reopened the issue with the data collected from different languages. Boroditsky’s team worked with the Kuuk Thaayorre people, an aboriginal Australian community, and they discovered that in the language, everything is expressed in cardinal directions: north, south, east, and west. Instead of using words like “left” and “right”, a Kuuk Thaayoreorre man would say “A tree is to the southeast of your house,” or “Move your chair to the northeast a little.” It comes as no surprise that in a language which requires the speaker to tell which way they are facing, people stay oriented — better oriented than speakers of other languages. Another dimension in which language shapes thought is relative to time. An English speaker would usually organize time from left to right, but with Arabic speakers, time is laid out from right to left. English speakers tend to talk about time using horizontal spatial metaphors (“The worst is behind us”), whereas Mandarin speakers have a vertical spatial metaphor of time (“down week” is “next week” and “up week” is “last week”). Besides abstract aspects like space time, language also influences basic cognitive conception such as color perception. Boroditsky’s lab compared Russian and English speakers’ ability to discriminate shades of blue. Unlike English, no single word covers all shades of the color blue in Russian; a Russian speaker makes an obligatory distinction between light blue (“goluboy”) and dark blue (“siniy”). As it turns out, Russian speakers are quicker to distinguish two shades of blue. Interestingly, when speakers looked at colors changing from light to dark blue, the brains of Russian speakers had a surprising reaction because the color had changed categorically.
